(is associated with: «Ukrainian diver suspected of Nord Stream attack arrested in Croatia») -/Danish Defence Command/dpa A Ukrainian national and trained diver was arrested on Wednesday morning in Croatia as a second suspect in the Nord Stream pipeline attacks of September 2022, the German public prosecutor's office said. The man, identified as Vladimir Z in compliance with Germany's privacy laws, was arrested in the city of Pula. He was detained by local police in coordination with the General Police Directorate in Zagreb, German prosecutors said. The man is "strongly suspected" of jointly causing an explosive to detonate as well as sabotage and destruction of structures, they said. Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement The man had previously been detained in Poland in September 2025. The Polish judiciary rejected a German extradition request at the time and released the suspect. The man is alleged to have participated as a trained diver in the diving operations in the Baltic Sea during which the explosive devices were placed on the gas pipelines, according to the public prosecutor's office. He and his accomplices are said to have used a sailing yacht that set out from Rostock. The yacht is alleged to have been hired from a German company via intermediaries using forged identity documents. The explosions near the Danish Baltic island of Bornholm in September 2022 severely damaged both Nord Stream pipelines, bringing gas flows to a complete halt. Before the attack, Nord Stream 1 transported Russian natural gas to Germany, while Nord Stream 2 had not yet entered service. Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Nobody has been held accountable for the attacks to date. In August last year, the alleged mastermind of the operation, Serhy K, was apprehended on Italy's Adriatic coast while on holiday with his family. The Public Prosecutor's Office filed charges against him at the Higher Regional Court in Hamburg in July. https://www.delfi.lt/en/politics/emergen.text: Delfi EN Delfi Politics 2026.08.24 19:01 Emergency declared in Kazlų Rūda municipality after storm Translated by Karolis Broga Source: Elta EN Emergency declared in Kazlų Rūda municipality after storm PHOTO: Ervin Rauluševičius | Elta Follow Delfi on Google Following a storm that swept the country last weekend, Kazlų Rūda municipality, located in central Lithuania, declared an emergency on Monday. Mayor Mantas Varaška says that around 1,200 households, which means around 3,000–4,000 people, are still without electricity supply. Many areas still have not been cleared of fallen trees and pose a risk. Therefore, access to some parks and recreation areas will be restricted. In addition, some residents have asked the municipality to provide drinking water, food and medicines. People in remote villages have been experiencing the power cut for two days. In some locations, telephone communications have been disrupted. As a result, the municipality has referred to the Ministry of National Defence requesting that the military would help. Other municipalities are also considering declaring a state of emergency. According to Anykščiai District Mayor Kęstutis Tubis, 9,755 households were still without power on Monday. He described the situation as bad. As a result of power cuts, water supply and wastewater treatment facilities are not operating in some areas of Anykščiai District. The mayor criticised electricity and natural gas distribution company Elektros skirstymo operatorius (ESO) for being inadequately prepared for disruptions of such extent. According to him, the company had more employees, vehicles and regional units in the past, whereas now it relies on contractors. "There should be more teams, more engineering services, electrical technicians who would deal with the consequences in such a situation," the mayor told ELTA. On Monday, 5,835 customers were still left without electricity in Šakiai District, which also affects operations of wastewater treatment plants. As a result, the municipality uses generators and, if needed, delivers drinking water tanks to residents. In Jonava Distrct, more than 8,000 consumers were without [pwer on Monday and the supply of drinking water is the biggest challenge. The local municipality is providing generators to water supply companies to ensure that drinking water is available in rural areas. However, declaring a state of emergency is not being considered in Jonava District. As reported, one person died and four were injured in a strong storm on Saturday, which fell trees and power lines. On Saturday night, around 268,000 households were left without power. By Monday morning, there were 129,000 households without electricity, mostly in Kaunas, Utena, Panevėžys and Vilnius region. A Polish priest who was injured in a deadly mass stabbing attack on a convent in southeast Poland last week called for "love" and "forgiveness" as he delivered his Saturday evening homily while wearing a bandage around his head, which remained visibly bruised. "No matter what happened, we must overcome the evil that happened here, in our abbey, with goodness, love, and forgiveness," Father Adrian Mantykiewicz told the congregation during his Sept. 26 homily at the Benedictine Abbey in Jaroslaw, Poland, where the knife attack had occurred two days earlier. "Therefore, I ask you to forgive, because it has affected all of you," he said, according to a transcript published by the Polish Jesuit news website DEON.pl. Police arrested a 31-year-old Ukrainian man for the attack, which killed one priest and sent four other people to the hospital. Father Stanislaw Zbojniewicz died at the hospital from his injuries, and Father Marek Pienkowski remains in serious condition in the hospital. Mantykiewicz told people not to blame the Ukrainian people because only one single person is responsible for the attack. He noted the convent — which is in a small town near the border with Ukraine — has provided support for many people who fled the Russia-Ukraine war. "From this place, I also want to ask you not to blame the nation from which the torturer belonged, because the evil was committed by a specific person, a specific person who has a name, a life, and is responsible for his actions," he said. "Other people did not do this. This was one, unique person." Mantykiewicz said he speaks in his own name and in the names of Zbojniewicz and Pienkowski when he says "very emphatically that we forgive and we ask you to pray for us." "For prayers for Father Stanislaw [Zbojniewicz], for the peace of his soul, for the health of Father Marek [Pienkowski], who is still fighting for his life in the hospital, and for me, that I may return to my duties as soon as possible and continue to serve you here," he said. The priest also asked people to pray for the attacker, specifically for "the grace of conversion," saying "he needs this prayer the most." He asked "not to respond to evil with evil but with love, support, understanding, and care" and to respect all people in the abbey, in the community, and in the country, including respect for Ukrainian refugees. Mantykiewicz said in his homily that "this sermon is difficult for me," but he said first and foremost, "I am a disciple of Jesus Christ, I am a disciple of my Master, I am a disciple of my Lord, and Christ teaches me to love." "Love that allowed itself to be crucified," he said. "Love that gave its life for its enemies. Such is my Lord and Master. And I am his servant." According to prosecutors, a man identified as Ihor M. faced charges for the attack. According to a statement , the investigation is ongoing, but he was charged with murder, attempted murder, and causing serious injury to victims. The suspect is receiving medical care, and prosecutors requested a public defender for him. He was appointed a Ukrainian translator. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq74.text: Figure caption, Watch: Trump says Musk has restored Ukraine's Starlink internet access after row By Gabriela Pomeroy Published 5 hours ago Elon Musk has restored Ukraine's Starlink internet access, US President Donald Trump has said after restrictions hampered Kyiv's armed forces. Trump made the comments after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said connectivity to the military-grade Starshield network, which is provided by Musk's satellite-based Starlink system, had yet to be fully restored. Musk previously denied he was behind the slowdown, which affects Ukraine's ability to use drones to attack Russia and protect itself from attacks. Trump refused to be drawn on a report that he had called Musk to ask him to lift restrictions to the service, but when asked about it he said: "Bottom line, he put it back." The Trump administration previously denied instructing Musk's company to restrict access. The connectivity restrictions came as Trump put pressure on Zelensky to stop attacking Russian oil refineries, which he has argued have caused prices to rise. Faced with midterm elections next month, Trump has waived some sanctions on Russia and agreed a deal to import Russian diesel for the US market - a move which has been criticised by Ukraine and its European allies. Image source, Reuters Image caption, A Ukrainian soldier using a Starlink satellite internet terminal which connects to thousands of SpaceX satellites Why is Starlink internet so important on the battlefield in Ukraine? Published 15 October Ukraine uses both the civilian service Starlink and the more secure Starshield, depending on what communications are needed. The networks use 10,000 satellites in low Earth orbit to provide connectivity, particularly in remote areas and battlefields. Modern warfare often relies on the use of high-speed internet to effectively operate drones. Earlier on Thursday, Zelensky said the speed of the system used by Ukraine's military had still not been restored fully. Speaking at a press conference, he said the speed "has not been restored to 400 [km/h; 250mph] yet", adding: "We are working on it." He continued: "I am waiting to hear from US Secretary of State [Marco] Rubio. He promised to get back to me with information within 48 hours or so." The Ukrainian president made the comments shortly before the Wall Street Journal , external reported that Trump called Musk and asked him to lift restrictions on Ukraine's use of Starlink. The US outlet reported that Trump told Musk he was frustrated the Starlink system's speeds were still capped at around 160km/h, according to officials. The speed limit made Ukraine's offensive drones and interceptors powerless against Russian attacks. The journal reported that the system was working more normally on Thursday, shortly after their conversation. BBC News has not confirmed the Wall Street Journal's report. It has also contacted the White House and SpaceX to ask for an explanation. Ukraine first reported an interruption to US intelligence sharing on 14 October. Musk said last week that the US government ultimately controls access to Starshield, the military-grade version of Starlink which Ukraine uses for some of its operation. He said the system was designed for the Pentagon, suggesting it may therefore be behind the restrictions. The White House has repeatedly said it did not order access to be restricted.
